problem: The caption says the wide-area link and the cloud 'sit on opposite sides of the device', but the graph has no device node at all: IoT is the centre, and both the cloud (3,3) and '5G and NB-IoT' (4,2) lie on the same upper-right side. A student reading the caption cannot match it to the picture.
fix: Caption: 'IoT sits at the centre of the technologies that make it possible. Sensors, RFID and embedded computing sit on the device side; networks, 5G/NB-IoT, cloud and analytics sit on the side that carries, stores and processes the data.'

problem: The example says the local gateway keeps its last reading during a power cut and uploads later. A power cut also removes power from the gateway and the home router, so the gateway would not be working; the benefit being illustrated is loss of the uplink, not loss of power.
fix: 'a Chennai flat loses its broadband link during a power cut; the local gateway, on its small battery, keeps the readings and uploads them when the link returns'.

problem: 'Fog computing is the older name for the same idea' overstates it. Standard usage treats edge computing as the broad term (computation at the device or the gateway) and fog computing as the specific layer of nodes between device and cloud; it is not just an earlier label for edge.
fix: 'Edge computing moves computation to the gateway or to the device itself. Fog computing is the related term for computation placed at intermediate nodes between the device and the cloud.'
